# Post drafts

## LinkedIn

I built a real-time equipment monitoring service, then used it to test a question I had written down in advance:
can it run on 8 sensors instead of 21?

The system: a Java 21 / Spring Boot service that streams NASA's C-MAPSS turbofan benchmark (a simulation, not
real engines) through Kafka. It keeps a sliding window per engine, scores remaining useful life with an
in-process ONNX model, and raises alerts that open once and close only when the condition has cleared.

The pre-registered answer was no. The 8 top-ranked sensors were {{ n.hyp_gap }} cycles worse than all 21, against
a {{ n.margin }}-cycle margin. So the service ships all 21.

The post hoc analysis was more interesting than the verdict:
- the 8 "best" sensors were near-copies of each other (correlation {{ n.redundancy_reduced8 }});
- 8 sensors chosen by forward selection came within {{ n.greedy8_gap }} cycles;
- the window length moved the error by about as much as the sensors did.

So the experiment said "no", and the ablations said "not like that".

Things that broke on the way, and the tests that caught them: an alert rule that fired on prediction jitter, a
score counted twice after a restart, a window saved to Redis before its score was written, and integration tests
leaking state into the dev database. In the end the processor was killed mid-stream, and
{{ n.restart_health_scores_rows }}/{{ n.restart_file_rows }} readings were scored exactly once.

Code, paper, a from-scratch tutorial and every number: github.com/Narenkaarthik/equipment-health-monitor

## Thread

1/ I wrote down a hypothesis before training anything: 8 sensors predict an engine's remaining life as well as 21.
Then I built a streaming service to test it.

2/ Setup: NASA C-MAPSS FD001 (simulated turbofans), engine-level split, {{ n.n_seeds }} seeds, the test set read once, and
every choice committed to a config file first.

3/ Result: rejected. The 8 ranked sensors were {{ n.hyp_gap }} cycles RMSE worse than all 21 ({{ n.main_gbr_full21_test_rmse }}).
The service ships 21.

4/ Post hoc: the ranked 8 were redundant (r = {{ n.redundancy_reduced8 }}). 8 chosen by forward selection: +{{ n.greedy8_gap }}.
It's which sensors, not how many.

5/ And the window length mattered about as much as the sensors. A verdict that depends on a recipe choice that
large is itself the finding.

6/ The service: Kafka keyed by machine, O(1) window features, ONNX checked against Python, alerts that open once.
I killed the processor mid-stream and lost nothing.

7/ The model was the small part. Most bugs lived in the system around it.
